messages.content: I want to develop robotic active perception that resolves occlusions relevant to grasping, while accounting for uncertain object motion caused by the sensing actions themselves. What is the core challenge here?

The robot needs information about parts of an object that are hidden but matter for a grasp. An action taken to obtain that information may also move the object, and the resulting motion is uncertain. The challenge is to improve grasp-relevant visibility without treating the object as though it must remain where it was before sensing.
So the aim is not simply to reveal as much of the object as possible?

Right. The stated aim is to resolve grasp-relevant occlusions. It does not require revealing every hidden surface or producing a complete view of the object. What matters is whether the perception gained helps address uncertainty relevant to grasping, while the possible effects of sensing on object motion remain part of the problem.
How should I state the grasp-performance requirement precisely?

The target is to reduce failed grasps by 20% relative to a fixed-view baseline under matched action budgets. That is a relative reduction in failed grasps, not a reduction of 20 percentage points. Matching the action budgets is part of the comparison; the requirement does not specify the precise budget or how actions are counted.
Does the fixed-view comparison mean active perception can be given more actions to achieve that reduction?

No. The 20% failed-grasp reduction is specified relative to the fixed-view baseline under matched action budgets. The comparison is therefore not meant to rely on giving the active-perception approach a larger action budget. Nothing here specifies a particular number of actions.
And what is the safety requirement alongside that?

Maintain object-damage rates below 1% across previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns. The threshold is strictly below 1%, and the requirement applies in the stated setting of previously unseen dynamics and occlusion patterns. Improving grasp performance does not replace this damage constraint.
Why mention object dynamics separately from occlusion patterns?

They describe different kinds of variation the approach must contend with. Occlusion patterns concern what grasp-relevant information is hidden; object dynamics concern how objects may move, including motion that a sensing action might induce. The requirement names both as previously unseen. It does not specify particular objects, motions, or occlusion arrangements.
Would it be accurate to assume a sensing action leaves the object in place until the grasp?

No. Accounting for uncertain object motion induced by sensing actions is an explicit part of the goal. A sensing action may change the object’s state, and its effect cannot simply be treated as known in advance. That is why gaining a better view and retaining a reliable basis for grasping have to be considered together.
Does that prescribe a particular way to predict or handle the motion?

No particular prediction method, sensing action, sensor, or control algorithm is specified. The requirement is at the level of the capability: the active-perception approach should take uncertainty about sensing-induced object motion into account rather than ignoring it.
If an approach clears an occlusion but causes more damage, would it still satisfy the objective?

Not if its object-damage rate fails to stay below 1% across the stated previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns. Resolving a grasp-relevant occlusion is part of the goal, but the damage threshold is a separate requirement that must also be maintained.
What if it is very gentle but does not improve grasp outcomes enough?

Then it would still need to meet the other stated requirement: 20% fewer failed grasps than the fixed-view baseline under matched action budgets. Low damage alone does not establish the specified grasp-performance improvement. Both requirements matter.
Is the 20% figure a result that has already been observed?

No result is stated here. The 20% relative reduction is a target for failed grasps, just as a damage rate below 1% is a target to maintain. The objective does not claim that either target has already been achieved.
Can I say how damage is measured, or whether the threshold is checked separately for every object?

Those details are not specified. You can retain the stated requirement—object-damage rates below 1% across previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns—without adding a damage definition or a particular aggregation rule. Specifying either would go beyond this objective.
Then the central tension is that sensing can help a grasp and also disturb what will be grasped?

Yes. Active perception is intended to resolve occlusions that matter for grasping, but the sensing actions may induce uncertain object motion. The approach must account for that interaction while pursuing at least a 20% reduction in failed grasps relative to a fixed-view baseline under matched action budgets and maintaining object-damage rates below 1% across previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns.

For the active-perception problem, I propose using risk-constrained belief-space MPC to select occlusion-clearing views or probes. The selection would use action-conditioned motion ensembles and a 0.5% damage-risk cap. How do these pieces fit together?

Belief-space MPC treats decisions as choices made under uncertainty, rather than as choices based on a single certain object state. Here, it would consider views or probes that could clear grasp-relevant occlusions while accounting for uncertain motion associated with each possible sensing action. Action-conditioned motion ensembles provide a way to represent differing possible motion outcomes for those actions. The risk constraint places a 0.5% cap on damage risk when selecting among them. This describes a proposed approach, not an observed performance result.
What does “action-conditioned” add to the motion ensembles?

It means the possible motion outcomes are considered in relation to the action being evaluated. A view and a probe need not have the same possible effects on the object, nor do two different candidate actions. Conditioning the ensemble on the candidate action helps avoid treating uncertain motion as a single, action-independent background uncertainty. The proposal does not specify how those ensembles are obtained or represented.
Why put the decision in belief space rather than reason from just one estimated object position?

A single estimated position can conceal uncertainty that matters for a grasp, especially when an occlusion leaves relevant details unresolved and a sensing action might move the object. Belief-space reasoning keeps that uncertainty in the decision. In this proposal, the point is to evaluate an occlusion-clearing action with both its possible information gain and its possible motion consequences in mind; no particular belief representation is specified.
Are views and probes two different objectives?

They are two kinds of candidate action in the same proposal: select occlusion-clearing views or probes. The shared purpose is to address occlusions relevant to grasping. The wording does not require both kinds of action to be used in every situation, and it does not define a particular viewing motion or probing technique.
Could the controller just choose whichever candidate reveals the most?

That would leave out important parts of the proposal. A candidate must be considered in light of action-conditioned uncertain motion and the 0.5% damage-risk cap, not just how much it might reveal. Also, the relevant aim is clearing grasp-relevant occlusions, not maximizing visibility for its own sake. The proposal does not specify a numerical information score or a particular rule for ranking candidates that satisfy the risk constraint.
Is MPC important here because the robot can reconsider its choice as information changes?

That is the usual idea behind model predictive control: make a decision using a forward-looking model, then reconsider as the available information changes. In belief space, that forward look also concerns uncertainty. The proposal names MPC but does not specify a planning horizon, an update schedule, or exactly how new observations would change the belief.
How would an ensemble affect the choice if one possible outcome is useful for visibility but another moves the object?

Conceptually, the choice should reflect both possibilities rather than assuming the useful outcome is certain. The action-conditioned ensemble is there to keep possible motion outcomes tied to the proposed action as the controller weighs whether it could clear the occlusion. The risk constraint then limits allowable damage risk. The proposal does not state how individual ensemble outcomes are weighted or converted into a damage-risk estimate.
Should I describe the 0.5% damage-risk cap as the same thing as the below-1% object-damage requirement?

No. The proposal specifies a 0.5% damage-risk cap for action selection; the broader goal specifies maintaining object-damage rates below 1% across previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns. They are related but distinct: one is a proposed risk constraint in the decision process, and the other is a performance requirement. Imposing the cap does not, by itself, establish what damage rate will be observed.
Because 0.5% is less than 1%, can I say the safety requirement is guaranteed?

No. The numerical cap is stricter than 1%, but a planned or estimated damage risk is not automatically the same as the resulting object-damage rate, particularly in previously unseen conditions. The proposal does not provide a guarantee that the below-1% requirement will be met.
Does the proposal specify whether 0.5% applies to each candidate action or to a whole planned sequence?

It specifies a 0.5% damage-risk cap, but not the exact unit over which that risk is calculated. I would avoid asserting a per-action, per-sequence, or cumulative interpretation without further specification. The faithful description is that risk-constrained belief-space MPC selects occlusion-clearing views or probes using action-conditioned motion ensembles, subject to that cap.
Could I describe the ensemble as learned from a particular class of objects?

Not from this proposal alone. It calls for action-conditioned motion ensembles but does not say how they are generated, what data they use, or which objects they cover. Those would be additional implementation claims.
How specifically does this proposal relate to the failed-grasp target?

It proposes a way to choose sensing actions that address grasp-relevant occlusions while taking sensing-induced motion and damage risk into account. That makes it relevant to the goal of reducing failed grasps by 20% relative to a fixed-view baseline under matched action budgets. The proposal itself does not claim that the reduction has been achieved or quantify its expected effect on failed grasps.
And the action budget—does this proposal set one?

No. The matched-action-budget condition belongs to the failed-grasp comparison, but this proposal does not set a budget, a number of views or probes, or a planning horizon. Those details should not be inferred from the use of MPC.
So, in plain language, what would the controller be deciding?

It would be deciding which occlusion-clearing view or probe to select while reasoning about uncertain object motion that could result from that choice and respecting a 0.5% damage-risk cap. “Belief-space MPC” names the uncertainty-aware, forward-looking decision framework; “action-conditioned motion ensembles” name the proposed representation of possible motion associated with candidate actions. The wording leaves the exact models and decision calculations open.
Would it be fair to say the probe is safe because the ensemble accounts for its motion?

No. Accounting for possible motion does not make a probe safe by definition. The ensemble is intended to inform the risk-constrained choice, and the 0.5% cap expresses a limit on damage risk in that choice. Whether the resulting approach actually maintains object-damage rates below 1% under previously unseen object dynamics and occlusion patterns remains a separate question.
I want to avoid making this sound like a completed experiment. What tense should I use?

Use proposal language: “Use risk-constrained belief-space MPC to select occlusion-clearing views or probes, using action-conditioned motion ensembles and a 0.5% damage-risk cap.” You can say what the components are intended to address, but avoid claiming that any grasp-failure reduction, damage rate, or generalization outcome has already been measured.
How can action-conditioned motion ensembles calibrate damage-risk estimates for unseen objects while selecting probes that reveal occluded grasp surfaces?

That is an open question for the proposed approach. An action-conditioned ensemble could represent several ways an object might move in response to each candidate probe, rather than assuming one outcome. To select a probe, the controller would need to consider both whether it might reveal an occluded grasp surface and whether its possible outcomes imply damage risk. Calibration asks a further question: when the controller assigns a level of damage risk, how well does that estimate correspond to what happens, including for unseen objects? The ensemble may inform the estimate, but it does not establish calibration by itself.
What is the distinction between predicting motion and calibrating damage risk?

Predicting motion concerns what the object might do after a particular probe. Estimating damage risk concerns the chance that the probe’s possible consequences damage it. Calibration concerns the reliability of that risk estimate: whether outcomes associated with a stated risk occur at a corresponding rate. Motion possibilities are relevant evidence, but motion and damage are not identical. The question leaves open how possible motion would be translated into a damage-risk estimate.
Why does conditioning on the probe matter for that estimate?

Because the uncertain motion is induced by the sensing action being considered. If different candidate probes could have different effects, a risk estimate that ignores which probe is selected could miss a consequential difference. Action conditioning ties the possible motion outcomes to each candidate. Whether the resulting estimates are well calibrated, especially for unseen objects, is still something to establish rather than assume.
Could the controller simply count the damaging outcomes in each motion ensemble?

Not without further assumptions. A motion outcome is not automatically labeled as damaging, and the proposal does not specify how damage would be identified from an outcome or how ensemble members would relate to probabilities. Counting alone would therefore not necessarily give a calibrated damage-risk estimate. Those gaps are central to the question, rather than details already settled by the word “ensemble.”
What makes unseen objects a particular difficulty?

For an unseen object, the controller may be less certain that its predicted responses to a probe capture what could actually happen. Even an estimate that appears precise could be misleading if the ensemble misses consequential motion or if the connection between motion and damage differs. The question is how to account for that uncertainty while still deciding whether a probe is worth taking to reveal a grasp surface; it does not state that a particular solution has been demonstrated.
Is a wider range of predicted motion the same as a higher damage risk?

Not necessarily. A wider range indicates uncertainty about motion, whereas damage risk concerns damaging outcomes. Greater motion uncertainty can make a risk estimate harder to trust, but it does not, by itself, say which outcomes cause damage or how likely they are. A calibrated approach would need to avoid conflating the spread of an ensemble with the probability of damage.
Then what does calibration contribute to probe selection?

It matters because a risk-constrained choice depends on the meaning of the risk number. If a candidate probe is estimated to be below a damage-risk cap but that estimate understates risk for unseen objects, the cap may not provide the intended protection. Conversely, a poorly grounded estimate could also discourage probes that might reveal an occluded grasp surface. Calibration is about making the risk estimate dependable enough to inform that tradeoff; it does not dictate a particular probe.
Should revealing the surface and estimating damage be treated as separate decisions?

They are distinct considerations, but the selection question brings them together for each candidate probe. The controller needs to consider what a probe might reveal about an occluded grasp surface and what uncertain motion and damage risk might accompany that same probe. Evaluating visibility alone would miss risk; evaluating risk alone would not address why the probe is being considered. The question does not prescribe a particular way to combine those considerations.
Does an ensemble need to predict the exact final object position to be useful?

The motivation for an ensemble is to represent uncertainty rather than commit to one exact motion outcome. It could be useful for comparing possible consequences of candidate probes even when the final position is uncertain. But usefulness for selection and calibration of damage risk are different claims. The question does not specify what prediction accuracy is required, or show that an ensemble with a given accuracy yields reliable risk estimates.
We proposed a 0.5% damage-risk cap earlier. Does calibration become especially important with such a cap?

Yes, conceptually: applying a 0.5% damage-risk cap relies on the estimated risk being meaningful near that limit. The cap is part of the proposed selection approach, while the question here is how to make estimates credible for unseen objects. Nothing stated here establishes that the estimates are calibrated at 0.5%, or that applying the cap guarantees the broader object-damage requirement.
Can I say the ensembles themselves will make that 0.5% estimate accurate?

That would be too strong. Action-conditioned ensembles can express possible motion associated with a probe, but their coverage of unseen-object responses and their connection to damage remain uncertain in the question. The issue is precisely how they can be used to calibrate risk estimates, not an assertion that calibration follows automatically from using them.
What would it mean for an estimate to be overconfident here?

It would mean the estimate conveys more certainty about low damage risk than is warranted by the possible outcomes for an unseen object. In practical terms, a probe could appear comfortably within a risk limit because relevant possibilities are missing or insufficiently reflected in the estimate. That is a conceptual failure mode, not a claim that it has occurred in this work.
Could being cautious about unseen objects prevent the robot from clearing an important occlusion?

It could create that tension. If uncertainty about damage risk makes a candidate probe hard to justify, the controller might forgo information about an occluded grasp surface. The question asks how to navigate that tension—select probes that reveal relevant surfaces without treating uncertain, potentially damaging effects as known to be safe. It does not specify where the balance should be set beyond the risk cap already proposed.
Is the question asking for a new motion model or for a way to use the ensemble in decisions?

Its wording centers on how action-conditioned motion ensembles can support calibrated damage-risk estimates for unseen objects while probes are selected to reveal occluded grasp surfaces. That encompasses the relationship between predicted motion, estimated damage risk, and probe choice. It does not commit to building a new motion model or identify a particular calibration procedure.
How should I phrase the unresolved part without implying we have an answer?

You could ask: “How can action-conditioned motion ensembles support well-calibrated damage-risk estimates for unseen objects when choosing probes to reveal occluded grasp surfaces?” That keeps both demands visible—risk estimates that remain meaningful for unseen objects and probes that address grasp-relevant occlusion—without claiming that the ensembles already achieve either one.

My hypothesis is that contact-stratified conformal calibration will keep unseen-object damage below 1%, while ensemble-guided probes cut occluded-grasp failures by at least 20% versus budget-matched fixed views. How should I explain the claim without presenting it as a result?

Present it as a prediction with two linked outcomes, not as something already demonstrated. The hypothesis is that contact-stratified conformal calibration will keep damage below 1% for unseen objects, and that ensemble-guided probes will reduce occluded-grasp failures by at least 20% compared with fixed views under matched action budgets. The proposed methods are named, but no observed damage rate or grasp-failure reduction is supplied.
What is the role of contact-stratified conformal calibration in that wording?

It names the proposed calibration approach associated with the damage claim. “Contact-stratified” indicates that contact distinctions matter to that calibration, rather than treating all contact situations as interchangeable. “Conformal calibration” identifies the proposed way of calibrating uncertainty. The hypothesis does not specify the contact strata, how they are defined, or the calibration procedure.
Does saying “conformal” mean I can claim the below-1% outcome is guaranteed?

No. The below-1% unseen-object damage outcome is the hypothesis. Naming conformal calibration does not, on its own, establish that outcome or a guarantee for unseen objects. Any guarantee would require conditions and a precise claim that are not stated here.
Why is contact stratification worth mentioning at all?

It is a specific feature of the hypothesized approach: calibration is to account for distinctions in contact. The wording suggests those distinctions could matter to damage-risk assessment, but it does not identify which distinctions matter or establish that stratifying by them improves safety. Those remain part of what the hypothesis puts forward.
Could I describe particular kinds of contact as the strata?
Not from this hypothesis alone. You can say the calibration is contact-stratified, but naming particular categories would add an implementation detail that has not been specified.
How do the ensemble-guided probes relate to the occluded-grasp part?

They are the proposed means of choosing probes in the presence of uncertain object motion. The hypothesis predicts that using those probes will cut failures on occluded grasps by at least 20% relative to budget-matched fixed views. It does not specify the individual probes, how the ensembles guide each choice, or an observed effect.
Does the hypothesis say every probe must reveal an occluded grasp surface?

No. Its performance claim concerns occluded-grasp failures under an ensemble-guided probing approach. The broader discussion motivates probes that reveal occluded grasp surfaces, but this hypothesis does not make a per-probe promise that every selected action will reveal one.
Is “at least 20%” meant to include exactly 20%?

Yes. “At least 20%,” or “≥20%,” includes exactly 20% and larger reductions. It is a relative comparison in occluded-grasp failures against budget-matched fixed views, not a claim of 20 percentage points.
What does budget-matched prevent me from implying?

It prevents framing the comparison as one in which the ensemble-guided probes receive a larger action budget than the fixed-view baseline. The hypothesis compares them under matched budgets. It does not specify the budget’s numerical size or precisely how actions are counted.
Should I shorten “occluded-grasp failures” to just “grasp failures”?
Keep “occluded-grasp failures” when stating this hypothesis. That is the outcome it names. Shortening it to all grasp failures could broaden the claim beyond what is stated.
Likewise, can I shorten “unseen-object damage below 1%” to “safe for all objects”?

No. The hypothesis specifies damage below 1% for unseen objects. “Safe for all objects” is broader and less precise, and it would conceal both the numerical threshold and the fact that this is a prediction rather than an established result.
Is a damage rate of exactly 1% consistent with the hypothesis?
No. “Below 1%” is strict: exactly 1% would not satisfy that part of the prediction. By contrast, exactly 20% would satisfy the “at least 20%” reduction in occluded-grasp failures.
Are the damage and failure claims alternatives—would meeting one be enough?

No. The hypothesis joins them: contact-stratified conformal calibration is predicted to keep unseen-object damage below 1%, while ensemble-guided probes are predicted to cut occluded-grasp failures by at least 20% versus budget-matched fixed views. Meeting only one would not establish the full hypothesis.
Could calibrated damage-risk estimates alone establish the damage part?

Not by themselves. Calibration concerns the reliability of risk estimates; the hypothesis makes a claim about damage for unseen objects. A well-described risk estimate is not automatically evidence that actual damage remains below 1%. The hypothesized connection between calibration and that outcome still has to be assessed.
Does the hypothesis claim that ensemble-guided probes cause no motion?

No. Ensemble guidance is relevant precisely because sensing actions can be associated with uncertain object motion. The hypothesis predicts a reduction in occluded-grasp failures from the probing approach; it does not say the probes leave objects stationary or eliminate uncertainty.
How much can I say about the relationship between the calibration and the probe selection?

You can say they are complementary parts of the hypothesis: contact-stratified conformal calibration is tied to the below-1% unseen-object damage prediction, and ensemble-guided probes are tied to the ≥20% occluded-grasp-failure reduction. The statement does not specify their exact interaction in a controller or claim that one outcome follows automatically from the other.
Could I call the hypothesis a tradeoff in which more damage is acceptable if failures fall enough?

No. The predicted failure reduction does not relax the damage condition. The hypothesis calls for both unseen-object damage below 1% and at least 20% fewer occluded-grasp failures relative to budget-matched fixed views.
What's a concise version that retains all of those qualifications?

“We hypothesize that contact-stratified conformal calibration will keep unseen-object damage below 1%, while ensemble-guided probes will reduce occluded-grasp failures by ≥20% compared with budget-matched fixed views.” That states the proposed methods, both numerical conditions, the comparison, and the fact that the outcomes remain hypothetical.

To evaluate the hypothesis, I want to run OccluMotion-2000 on held-out dynamics and occlusions, comparing conformally calibrated probes against budget-matched fixed views for damage and grasp-failure rates. How should I describe the activity?

Describe it as a planned comparison: run OccluMotion-2000 under held-out dynamics and occlusions, then compare the damage rates and grasp-failure rates of conformally calibrated probes with those of budget-matched fixed views. The activity specifies what to compare and under which held-out conditions; it does not report an outcome.
What do the held-out dynamics and occlusions contribute to the comparison?

They make the comparison address dynamics and occlusion patterns not included in the corresponding non-held-out conditions. That is pertinent to the question of how the approach behaves beyond familiar conditions. The activity does not identify particular dynamics or occlusion patterns, or specify how they are held out.
Does “held-out dynamics and occlusions” also mean the objects themselves are held out?

Not necessarily. The activity explicitly says held-out dynamics and occlusions; it does not separately specify an object holdout. I would preserve that wording rather than assume a particular split of objects.
And is OccluMotion-2000 necessarily a set of 2,000 trials?
The name alone does not establish its size or the number of trials. You can name OccluMotion-2000 as the setting to run, but should not infer a trial count from “2000.”
Why compare against fixed views rather than discussing the probe rates on their own?

The fixed-view condition supplies the stated comparison for both damage and grasp-failure rates. Rates for the probes alone would not show how they compare with budget-matched fixed views. The activity does not specify any other comparison condition.
Does budget-matched mean both conditions must perform the same actions?

No. The comparison is between probes and fixed views, so the actions need not be identical. “Budget-matched” means the comparison is made under matched budgets, rather than giving one condition more action budget. The activity does not specify the budget’s size or the counting convention.
What exactly should be compared on the safety side?

The stated safety-side outcome is damage rate. Compare that rate for conformally calibrated probes and budget-matched fixed views under the held-out dynamics and occlusions. The activity does not provide a definition of damage or any measured rate.
And on the grasping side?

Compare grasp-failure rates for the same two conditions. Together with damage rates, that lets the planned activity examine both outcomes named in the comparison. No grasp-failure rate or difference between conditions has yet been stated.
Should I say the test will prove conformal calibration keeps damage low?

No. The run is intended to evaluate the hypothesis, not to guarantee its outcome in advance. It compares a conformally calibrated probe condition with budget-matched fixed views and measures damage and grasp-failure rates. The activity by itself does not establish that calibration keeps damage below any threshold.
Does this activity spell out how the probes are conformally calibrated?

No. It identifies the condition as “conformally calibrated probes” but does not describe the calibration procedure, its inputs, or how it affects probe selection. Those details should not be supplied as though they were part of this activity.
Can I call the probes contact-stratified in the activity description?

The hypothesis names contact-stratified conformal calibration, while this activity describes the compared condition as conformally calibrated probes. You can identify the activity as an evaluation of that hypothesis, but the activity’s own wording does not spell out the stratification or its implementation. For a precise description of the run, retain “conformally calibrated probes.”
Would one rate be enough if it showed a strong difference?
No. The planned comparison explicitly covers both damage and grasp-failure rates. A difference in one would not, by itself, state what happened to the other.
Can I say already that probes outperform the fixed-view baseline?

No. This node says to run the comparison; it contains no results. Whether the probes have lower grasp-failure rates, how their damage rates compare, or whether either meets a target remains unanswered here.
Does the plan specify a particular number of grasp attempts, objects, or repetitions?

It does not. Nor does it specify whether OccluMotion-2000 is conducted in simulation or with physical objects. Those details cannot be inferred from the activity’s name or from the instruction to compare rates.
What is the most faithful one-sentence description?

“Run OccluMotion-2000 on held-out dynamics and occlusions, comparing conformally calibrated probes with budget-matched fixed views on damage rates and grasp-failure rates.” That retains the planned run, its held-out conditions, both comparison groups, the budget match, and both outcomes without implying that results are already known.
What did the OccluMotion-2000 comparison show?
On OccluMotion-2000, contact-calibrated probes reduced held-out grasp failures from 20% with budget-matched fixed views to 15%. The reported damage rate was 0.4%.
Is that a five percent reduction in grasp failures?
It is a reduction of 5 percentage points, from 20% to 15%. Relative to the fixed-view failure rate of 20%, the reduction is 25%: five divided by twenty.
Why specify that the fixed views were budget-matched?

It identifies the basis of the grasp-failure comparison. The 20% fixed-view rate and 15% contact-calibrated-probe rate were compared under matched action budgets, rather than attributing a difference to one condition having a larger budget. The evidence does not state the budget’s size.
Does the 0.4% figure describe damage in both conditions?

The evidence reports damage as 0.4% alongside the contact-calibrated-probe result. It does not give a separate damage rate for budget-matched fixed views, so there is no stated damage-rate difference between the two conditions.
Can I describe the held-out cases more specifically?

The comparison was run on OccluMotion-2000 with held-out dynamics and occlusions, but the reported result does not identify particular dynamics or occlusion patterns. It also does not specify a separate object holdout. Those details should not be inferred from the phrase “held-out grasp failures.”
Do we know how many grasp attempts went into the percentages?

No count is given. The percentages state the reported rates, but not the number of attempts, repetitions, or uncertainty around the estimates. The “2000” in OccluMotion-2000 should not be treated as a trial count on its own.
Does this result tell us how the contact calibration changed individual probe choices?

No. It reports outcomes for contact-calibrated probes, not the calibration procedure or a trace of individual decisions. It does not isolate which part of the approach produced the difference in grasp-failure rates.
What is the cleanest way to report both the absolute and relative grasp-failure changes?

“On OccluMotion-2000, held-out grasp failures fell from 20% for budget-matched fixed views to 15% for contact-calibrated probes—a 5-percentage-point, or 25% relative, reduction. The reported damage rate was 0.4%.”
Given that held-out grasp failures fell 25% while damage remained 0.4%, what decision should we make about contact-calibrated probing?

Advance contact-calibrated probing to the next validation stage. The stated basis for that decision is the 25% reduction in held-out grasp failures alongside a 0.4% damage rate. Advancement is a decision to continue validation, not a claim that further validation has already taken place.
Should I describe this as approving it for deployment?
No. The decision is specifically to advance contact-calibrated probing to the next validation stage. Deployment would be a different decision, and none is stated here.
What does “next validation stage” tell us about what happens next?
It tells us that validation is to continue, but it does not specify the next stage’s setting, tests, criteria, or schedule. The decision should not be expanded into a particular validation plan.
Is the 25% figure the reduction in the damage rate?
No. The 25% decrease refers to held-out grasp failures. Damage is reported separately at 0.4%; the decision does not state a percentage reduction in damage.
And does “damage remained 0.4%” mean it was 0.4% in every condition?

No. It states the damage figure accompanying the decision to advance contact-calibrated probing. It does not give damage rates for every comparison condition or say that every individual case had that rate.
Could I say the decision follows from the grasp-failure improvement alone?

That would leave out part of its stated rationale. The decision cites both the 25% drop in held-out grasp failures and damage remaining at 0.4%. Keep both figures when explaining why contact-calibrated probing is being advanced.
Does advancing it mean we know how it will perform in the next stage?
No. The decision authorizes moving to further validation; it does not report outcomes from that stage or predict specific rates there. The 25% and 0.4% figures are the stated grounds for advancing.
Can I call this a decision about contact-calibrated probing generally, or must I name a particular probe?
Call it a decision to advance contact-calibrated probing. No individual probe or probe-selection rule is identified in the decision, so naming one would add an unsupported detail.
What is a concise statement of the decision and its reason?
“Advance contact-calibrated probing to the next validation stage: held-out grasp failures fell 25%, while damage remained 0.4%.”
What is the validation plan after advancement?

After advancement, test 500 novel-dynamics grasps under unseen occlusions against budget-matched fixed views. The plan is to verify at least 20% fewer failed grasps relative to the fixed-view comparison and an object-damage rate below 1%. These are criteria to check, not results from the planned test.
What does “500 novel-dynamics grasps” tell us, and what does it leave open?

It gives the planned number of grasps and says they will involve novel dynamics. It does not identify those dynamics, say that the objects themselves are novel, or specify how the 500 grasps are allocated between the approach being tested and fixed views.
Why mention unseen occlusions separately?

The plan calls for testing under both novel dynamics and unseen occlusions. Those are distinct conditions: how an object may move is not the same as what grasp-relevant information is hidden. The plan does not specify particular motion behaviors or occlusion patterns.
Is the fixed-view condition just background context, or part of the test?

It is the stated comparison condition. The plan calls for testing against budget-matched fixed views so that the failed-grasp reduction can be assessed relative to that baseline. It does not specify the numerical action budget or how actions will be counted.
Does budget-matched mean the approach being tested and the fixed-view condition have to choose identical actions?
No. Their actions can differ; the requirement is that their action budgets match. The plan does not define a particular set of actions for either condition.
How exactly should I read “at least 20% fewer failures”?

It is a relative reduction of at least 20% in failed grasps compared with budget-matched fixed views. Exactly 20% meets that criterion; it does not mean a reduction of 20 percentage points. The plan does not state what either failure rate will be.
And is a damage rate of exactly 1% acceptable?
